title.en: Korean Temple Food in Seoul: The Rules, the Bowl Ritual and Where to Try It

summary.en: Korean temple food leaves out meat, fish and five pungent plants. What the four-bowl meal means, how it differs from vegan food, and where to cook or eat it in Seoul.

guide.audience: Visitors to Seoul, vegetarian or not, who want to understand Korean Buddhist temple food and then cook or eat it properly without committing to a Templestay.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Class schedules, opening hours and booking rules change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: Korean temple food (사찰음식, sachal eumsik) uses no meat or fish and none of the five pungent plants, garlic and green onion among them, and takes its flavor from fermented soy, mushrooms, kelp and the season. In Seoul, cook it with a monk at the Korean Temple Food Culture Experience Center in Anguk-dong, which offers English interpretation on Friday and Saturday mornings, or book a set course at Balwoo Gongyang opposite Jogyesa, which closes on Sundays.

en.heading: Two rules decide what reaches a monastery table
paragraphs: 사찰음식 (sachal eumsik) means food as it is cooked and eaten in Buddhist temples, and since May 19, 2025 it has been a National Intangible Heritage of Korea. The Korea Heritage Service listed it as a community item and named no individual master, because every temple keeps its own recipes and monks and nuns pass them on collectively. The designation covers both the everyday meals of monastic practice and balwoo gongyang (발우공양), the formal way of eating from nested bowls described below.

The first rule is the precept against taking life. The Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism, the Jogye Order body that runs the national temple-food program, explains it with a line from the Nirvana Sutra: eating meat cuts off the seed of compassion. Its own definition is worth reading closely. It excludes every animal food except dairy products, so meat, fish, eggs and fish-based stocks are out, while milk is not forbidden in principle.

The second rule removes the five pungent plants, osinchae (오신채): green onion, garlic, chives, wild chives called dallae, and heunggeo, a pungent plant that English sources translate as asafoetida or Chinese squill. Monastic teaching holds that their effect on the body gets in the way of meditation, and that strong seasoning feeds a small attachment to taste. Take away both meat and the onion family, and a cook has to make vegetables, grains and beans taste of themselves. That constraint, more than any single recipe, is what defines the cuisine.

The written record is long. The heritage service's designation announcement cited a Goryeo-dynasty collection of writings that mentions vegetarian dumplings and kimchi, and a Joseon-era diary showing temples supplying tofu, fermented soybean blocks (meju) and preserved foods, which they traded with scholar-official households for grain. Temples, in other words, were not only kitchens for monks but producers of the fermented basics that ordinary Korean cooking still depends on.

en.heading: Balwoo gongyang: four bowls, a bamboo clapper and nothing wasted
paragraphs: Balwoo (발우) are the wooden bowls a monk eats from, and gongyang (공양) means a meal offered and received. A standard set has four bowls of slightly different sizes that nest into one: the largest for rice, then soup, side dishes, and a bowl of clean water called cheonsu. Temple tradition traces the set to the Buddha himself, who is said to have received four stone bowls from the Four Heavenly Kings after his enlightenment and stacked them together.

The meal runs to the sound of a jukbi (죽비), a split bamboo clapper. At its signals the bowls are unwrapped and laid out, and servers bring water, rice, soup and side dishes in that order. Each person first rinses the bowls with the clean water, takes only as much food as they will finish, and recites the Five Contemplations, the ogwange (오관게). In plain terms it asks where the food came from, whether one's conduct deserves it, and resolves to let go of greed, to treat the meal as medicine for the body and to accept it in order to complete the path.

Eating is silent, at the same pace as everyone else. A few grains of rice are set aside as an offering for hungry beings, and one piece of kimchi is kept back until the end. Then a little water goes into the bowl, the kimchi is used to wipe it clean, and both are eaten and drunk. The bowls are rinsed again with the clean water, which is collected and should be clear enough to show that nothing was left behind.

The Cultural Corps sums up the spirit in five words: equality, because everyone receives the same food; cleanliness; frugality; community, since the whole assembly eats from one pot at one time; and merit, in gratitude to everyone who grew and cooked the food. For a visitor, this explains two things you will notice at any temple meal: portions are small, and leaving food on your plate is the one genuinely rude thing you can do.

en.heading: Seasonings from jars, hillsides and the calendar
paragraphs: Temple kitchens avoid artificial flavor enhancers and build depth from natural powders instead. The Cultural Corps lists the classics: ground dried mushrooms, ground kelp, jepi (a citrusy Korean pepper), perilla seed and raw soybean flour, stirred into broths, seasoned greens, braises and kimchi. Because fish sauce and salted shrimp are ruled out along with garlic, even temple kimchi tastes cleaner and sharper than the version most visitors know.

The backbone is jang (장), the fermented soy sauce, soybean paste and chili paste that temples have long made in rows of earthenware jars on a sunny terrace, the jangdokdae. In December 2024 UNESCO inscribed the knowledge, beliefs and practices of Korean jang-making on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, which makes the jars in a temple courtyard a living exhibit of two heritage listings at once. When the heritage service designated temple food, it singled out this reliance on fermented and local ingredients as part of what sets Korean temple food apart from that of other countries.

The menu follows the season as closely as it follows the precepts. The December 2026 special classes posted by Hyangjeoksegye, the order's temple-food education center, make the point: one session builds a winter table from sea vegetables, including rice cooked with hijiki and a seasoned salad of maesaengi seaweed and sweet potato; another turns to winter roots, starting with lotus-root rice; a two-day class makes rice syrup and uses it in turnip pickles and burdock braise; and one is devoted to making soybean pastes, including cheonggukjang. None of these is a fixed restaurant menu; they show how a temple cook reads the month.

Set your expectations accordingly. A temple meal tastes quieter than the garlic-and-chili Korean food you have probably eaten so far, and the first few dishes can seem mild. Give it a few mouthfuls. The pleasure lies in texture and contrast: the bitterness of a mountain green against a sweet glazed root, the deep salt of an old soybean paste against plain rice.

en.heading: Not simply vegan: where the two diverge
paragraphs: Temple food and vegan food overlap heavily, but they start from different questions. Veganism asks whether a product comes from an animal. Temple cooking asks whether it took a life, and whether it disturbs a mind in meditation. That is why the Cultural Corps' definition allows dairy in principle, and why VisitKorea's own guide to the cuisine says the same. If you avoid all animal products, ask about dairy, and about honey if you avoid that too, before you assume a temple dish is vegan.

The bigger practical difference runs the other way. Vegan cooking happily uses garlic, onions, leeks and chives, and much Korean vegan food is built on them. Temple cooking leaves out all five pungent plants. If you cannot eat garlic or onion, for medical or religious reasons, temple food is one of the few Korean cuisines where that is the rule rather than a special request.

For vegetarians, the most useful point is what temple food cannot contain. Ordinary Korean side dishes that look meat-free often are not: kimchi is commonly seasoned with fish sauce or salted shrimp, and soups and stews often start from anchovy stock. A cook following temple rules uses kelp and mushroom broth instead. That makes a properly run temple-food kitchen the most reliable meal in Seoul for anyone who avoids fish.

Our judgment: vegans and vegetarians should treat one temple meal as the safest special meal of a Seoul trip, and confirm dairy with a single question. Travelers who eat everything should go for the ritual and the flavors rather than for health claims, and should pair the meal with a temple visit so the food makes sense in its setting.

en.heading: Cooking with a monk near Anguk Station
paragraphs: The Korean Temple Food Culture Experience Center (한국사찰음식문화체험관) is run by the Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism and calls itself Korea's first multipurpose space devoted to temple food. It occupies the second floor of the Anguk Building annex at 39 Yulgok-ro, in Anguk-dong, and opens Tuesday to Sunday from 09:00 to 18:00. It closes on Mondays and public holidays, and between 11:30 and 13:00 staff are preparing classes and do not take inquiries.

Even without a booking, the open area is worth twenty minutes before or after a visit to Jogyesa. It displays models of temple dishes and a set of traditional balwoo bowls, lets you copy out the Five Contemplations by hand, runs an exhibition quiz with a small prize, and features an ingredient of the month to see, smell and touch. There are also books on temple food, free Wi-Fi and seats.

The classes are the real draw. Each is a single session led by a monk or nun: a short talk and cooking demonstration, then hands-on cooking in groups of four. Programs open to foreign participants come with English interpretation, and the center schedules them on Friday and Saturday mornings. A typical example is the Friday, November 27, 2026 session, labeled F-Temple Food and open to Korean and foreign participants together, which runs 10:00 to 11:30, cooks burdock japchae and napa cabbage wraps with soybean paste, takes 16 people and costs 20,000 won. Booking and payment are online only, and refunds are possible up to three days before the class.

Come prepared, because the center provides no disposables. Bring two kitchen cloths, a bag for the damp ones, a pen, and a container of about 600 milliliters for each dish, since you take the food away rather than eating it there. Aprons and a printed copy of the Five Contemplations are provided. Photos are fine as long as other participants are not in the frame, but video is not allowed. Arrive ten minutes early. Choose a class over a restaurant if you want to understand the cooking; plan to eat your results as a picnic or back at your room.

en.heading: Balwoo Gongyang and other tables in Seoul
paragraphs: Balwoo Gongyang (발우공양), named after the monastic meal, is the temple-food restaurant run directly by the Cultural Corps. It is on the fifth floor of the Templestay Information Center at 56 Ujeongguk-ro, the grey building directly opposite Jogyesa; the restaurant gives it as about three minutes from Anguk Station Exit 6 and seven from Jonggak Station Exit 3-1. It was listed in the Michelin Guide Seoul from 2017 to 2019, and GQ Korea's February 2026 round-up of temple-food restaurants confirms it is still serving.

It is a set-course restaurant. VisitKorea lists four courses named Seon (meditation), Won (vow), Maeum (mind) and Hee (joy), built on seasonal ingredients, and the dining rooms are divided into tables for four and six, group rooms and private rooms. Service runs Monday to Saturday: lunch from 11:30 in two sittings, a break from 15:00 to 18:00, then dinner. It is closed on Sundays. Check current prices and sittings on its website and reserve ahead, especially for a weekend lunch.

Choose it for a quiet, unhurried meal that shows the cuisine at its most refined; lunch fits naturally into a morning at Jogyesa and the experience center. Skip it if you want the austerity of an actual temple meal, because a restaurant course is plated and paced for diners, not for practice. For that, book a Templestay that includes a formal monastic meal; our temple guide explains the formats.

Farther out, in Eunpyeong-gu in Seoul's northwest, VisitKorea's temple-food feature includes Jinkwansa (진관사, also spelled Jingwansa), a temple worth combining with a walk if you want temple food in a mountain setting; check eng.templestay.com for its current programs. Elsewhere, restaurants describing themselves as 사찰음식 vary in how strictly they follow the rules. Before ordering, ask 오신채 들어가요? (osinchae deureogayo?, does it contain the pungent plants?) and name meat and fish separately.

en.heading: Eating like a guest at a temple table
paragraphs: At a Templestay meal or any formal temple lunch, follow the people around you and keep to a few principles. Take small portions, because you are expected to finish everything, down to the last grain of rice and the sauce. Eat quietly, without chatter or phone screens, and try to keep pace with the group rather than racing ahead or lingering. If the meal is a full balwoo gongyang, watch the person next to you and copy each step at the sound of the clapper; nobody expects a first-timer to know the order.

In a restaurant the formality relaxes, but two habits still matter. Ask about ingredients before you order rather than leaving dishes untouched afterward, and treat leftovers as the guest's failure, not the kitchen's. It is also courteous to say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgetseumnida) before eating and 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida) after, the ordinary Korean thanks for a meal, which carries more weight at a temple table than almost anywhere else.
checklist: 고기나 생선 들어가요? (gogina saengseon deureogayo?) Does it contain meat or fish?
오신채 들어가요? (osinchae deureogayo?) Does it contain the five pungent plants?
우유나 꿀 들어가요? (uyuna kkul deureogayo?) Does it contain milk or honey?
조금만 주세요 (jogeumman juseyo) Just a little, please.
잘 먹겠습니다 / 잘 먹었습니다 Thanks before and after the meal.

en.heading: A temple-food Saturday around Jogyesa
paragraphs: This plan needs a Saturday with an English-interpreted morning class; check the center's program list a few weeks ahead, since sessions have limited places. Start at Jogyesa (조계사) around 09:15 and watch the morning activity in the courtyard before the crowds arrive; our temple guide explains how to read the main hall and its etiquette. Walk on to the experience center in Anguk-dong in time to arrive ten minutes before a 10:00 class, containers and cloths in your bag.

After the class, around 11:30, spend a few minutes in the center's open exhibition area, copying out the Five Contemplations, the verse recited before every formal temple meal. Then stroll through Insadong, keeping your cooked dishes for later. Book the second lunch sitting at Balwoo Gongyang, which starts at 13:30, back opposite Jogyesa, and compare a chef's plated version of the cuisine with the home-style dishes you have just made.

Spend the afternoon at a traditional teahouse in Insadong, or, if the weather is good, take the subway to Bongeunsa and walk its grounds as the light drops. In the evening, eat the food from your morning class at your hotel or as a picnic. A Friday works the same way. Avoid Mondays, when the experience center is closed, and Sundays, when the restaurant is.

faq.q: Is Korean temple food vegan?
faq.a: Usually, but not by definition. Temple cooking excludes meat, fish and eggs, and the Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism defines it as excluding all animal foods except dairy. Most dishes are plant-based, but if you avoid dairy or honey, ask before ordering. Unlike most vegan cooking, it also leaves out garlic, green onion and the rest of the onion family.

faq.q: Can I take a temple cooking class in English in Seoul?
faq.a: Yes. The Korean Temple Food Culture Experience Center in Anguk-dong offers English interpretation for programs open to foreign participants, scheduled on Friday and Saturday mornings. Sessions are short, usually 90 minutes to two hours, led by a monk or nun, and booked and paid for online only. A November 2026 example cost 20,000 won.

faq.q: Why does temple food avoid garlic and onions?
faq.a: Buddhist monastic teaching treats the five pungent plants, osinchae, as stimulants that disturb meditation, and their strong flavors as a source of attachment to taste. The five are green onion, garlic, chives, wild chives and heunggeo. Temple cooks use mushrooms, kelp, perilla, jepi pepper and fermented soy instead.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation at Balwoo Gongyang?
faq.a: Reserving is strongly advisable. The restaurant serves set courses in fixed lunch sittings and at dinner from Monday to Saturday, and it closes on Sundays. Its website lists current sittings and contact details, and it is directly opposite Jogyesa on the fifth floor of the Templestay Information Center.

faq.q: Can I eat a monastic meal without staying overnight?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some one-day Templestay programs include a temple meal, and overnight programs usually include a formal balwoo gongyang. Search eng.templestay.com with the Temples for Foreigners filter and read each program's schedule, since meals vary by temple and season. A restaurant course is easier to book but is not the same ritual.

title.en: Seoul City Wall Hike: Four Mountain Sections, Gates and Bugaksan Access

summary.en: Hiking Hanyangdoseong, Seoul's 1396 city wall: the four mountain sections compared, 24-hour Bugaksan access, the old gates, the free certificate and winter safety.

guide.audience: Visitors with a free morning or afternoon who want to walk part of Seoul's Joseon-era city wall and need to choose a section, understand what they are seeing and do it safely.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Trail access, hours and certificate rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: For a first walk, take the Naksan section from Hyehwamun down to Heunginjimun: about an hour on gentle paths, best toward sunset. For a real hike, cross Baegak (Bugaksan) from Changuimun, 4.7 km and about three hours of steep stairs. It no longer needs ID or a permit: the city lists it as open 24 hours, every day, with recommended hours of 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February.

en.heading: A wall drawn along four mountains in 1396
paragraphs: When the Joseon dynasty made Hanyang its capital, King Taejo enclosed it in 1396 with a wall that follows the ridges of the four inner mountains, the naesasan: Baegak (also called Bugaksan) to the north, Naksan to the east, Mongmyeoksan, today's Namsan, to the south, and Inwangsan to the west. The result is a loop of roughly 18.6 kilometers, 5 to 8 meters high, and the Seoul Metropolitan Government notes that it served as a working capital wall for 514 years, from 1396 to 1910, longer than any other surviving capital-city wall in the world.

The wall marked the boundary and authority of the capital as much as it defended it. It had four main gates, Sukjeongmun to the north, Heunginjimun to the east, Sungnyemun to the south and Donuimun to the west, and four smaller ones: Changuimun, Hyehwamun, Gwanghuimun and Souimun. Two water gates south of Heunginjimun let streams drain out of the city. Donuimun and Souimun no longer exist, so two gates of the eight are now only names on street signs and markers.

The builders divided the whole circuit into 97 sections and named them in order after the characters of the Thousand Character Classic, starting with 天 (cheon, heaven) at the summit of Baegak. Workers from the same county were assigned the same stretch, and on many stones they carved the name of their county and section, an early form of accountability you can still read. The city calls the walking route 순성길 (sunseonggil), from sunseong, going around the wall.

en.heading: Reading the stones: rebuilds, losses and a UNESCO bid
paragraphs: The wall you walk is three Joseon walls layered on each other. In 1396 the flat stretches were rammed earth and only the mountain stretches were stone. In 1422 King Sejong replaced the earthen sections with stone, and in 1704 King Sukjong carried out another large rebuilding after sections had collapsed. Each campaign cut and laid its stones differently, so the shape and size of the blocks change from one stretch to the next; the official trail notes point to the path behind the Catholic University of Korea on Naksan as a good place to compare them.

The heaviest losses came with modernization. Trams arrived in 1899, the wall beside the main gates was pulled down for traffic from 1907, and under Japanese colonial rule Donuimun and Souimun were demolished and Gwanghuimun and Hyehwamun badly damaged. Restoration began around Sukjeongmun after the North Korean commando raid of January 21, 1968, and spread to the whole wall from 1974. As of 2022 the city counted about 14.5 kilometers, some 78 percent, as preserved or restored.

The wall is now part of a World Heritage bid. Under the name Capital Fortifications of Hanyang, Korea is nominating it together with Bukhansanseong, the mountain refuge fortress to the north, and Tangchundaeseong, the wall that linked the two. The Korea Heritage Service selected it as the country's nomination in July 2025, the official timeline set the full dossier for submission by February 1, 2026, and an evaluation mission by ICOMOS, UNESCO's heritage advisers, was expected between August and October 2026. Until a decision is announced, it is a nominated site, not a listed one.

en.heading: Four mountains, four very different walks
paragraphs: The city says the whole loop can be walked in a day, but it recommends splitting it into sections. Its Korean trail pages describe four, each named for a mountain, and fold the flat stretches around Heunginjimun and Sungnyemun, where most of the wall vanished under roads and buildings, into the Naksan and Namsan sections. The English pages list those two flat stretches as separate sections, so you will see both six-part and four-part maps.

Difficulty is the real dividing line. Baegak and Inwangsan are rated hardest, with long flights of stone steps, exposed rock and no shops; Naksan is the easiest, and Namsan sits in between. Add the four official times together and the full circuit comes to about ten and a half hours of walking, which is why most visitors choose one section and pair it with the neighborhood at either end.

en.heading: Baegak (Bugaksan): no ID, no permit, open around the clock
paragraphs: Baegak, 342 meters, was the principal mountain of the old capital in geomantic terms and the highest of the four. After a North Korean special forces unit infiltrated Seoul on January 21, 1968, the mountain was closed to the public for nearly forty years and reopened only in 2007. If an older guide tells you to bring a passport and register at an information post, it is out of date. The city's official trail page now lists the section as open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, on a self-entry basis, and marks the Changuimun and Malbawi information centers as closed.

The city still publishes recommended hours, and they are worth following on a mountain of long, steep staircases: 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February, 07:00 to 18:00 in March, April, September and October, and 07:00 to 19:00 from May to August. On October 17, 2026, the last closed part of the mountain opened as well: a 1.32-kilometer trail on the southwest slope from the Dolphin Rest Area above Changuimun, past Manse-dongbang, a rock inscription wishing the king long life, to the pine named after the 1968 raid, with four new lookouts.

Some restrictions remain because military facilities are still on the mountain. Photography and filming are restricted around military facilities, and signs mark where; follow them. Stay on the marked trails, and do not feed or approach the spotted deer that live on the slopes. Expect stairs almost all the way from Changuimun to the summit stone at Baegangmaru: the city built the climb entirely as steps for safety, which makes it hard on knees but not technical.

The rewards are the best wall scenery in Seoul. From Baegangmaru the view runs down over Gyeongbokgung and Sejong-daero, and the curved bastion called Baegak gokseong is the place to see how the wall rides the mountains around the city. Farther east, Sukjeongmun, the north gate, is the only surviving gate still joined to the wall on both sides; its gate tower was built new in 1976. Below it, at the Malbawi viewpoints, the trail splits toward Samcheong Park, Waryong Park and the information posts, so read the signs carefully.

en.heading: Naksan at dusk: the right section for a first walk
paragraphs: Naksan, at 124 meters the lowest of the four mountains, was nicknamed Naktasan, camel mountain, for its humped shape, and its gentle slope makes it the section to start with. Begin at Hyehwamun, the northeast gate, a few minutes from Hansung University Station Exit 5 on Line 4. The gate began in 1396 as Honghwamun, took its present name in 1511, lost its tower in 1928 and was rebuilt in 1994 slightly north of its original site.

Walk south with the wall beside you. Behind the Catholic University you can compare the stones of different centuries, then the path passes Jangsu Village outside the wall, a postwar settlement whose residents chose regeneration over redevelopment, before reaching Naksan Park, known for sunset and night views. Ihwa Village, just inside the wall, has been covered in murals and installations since 2006. People live in all of these lanes, and the city asks walkers to keep their voices down.

The descent passes Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park, where stones inscribed with builders' names and districts are most commonly found, and ends at Heunginjimun, the east gate. The present gate dates from 1869, and it has an extra outer wall because the east side, on the city's lowest ground, was the hardest to defend; the wall on either side was removed in 1907. Allow about an hour for the whole stretch.

Before the gate, stop at the Seoul City Wall Museum (한양도성박물관), which tells the story of the wall's construction, management, destruction and restoration, with a model of the whole circuit and a digital tour. It is free and open Tuesday to Sunday from 09:00 to 18:00, closed on Mondays and January 1, and it is near Dongdaemun Station Exit 1 on Line 1 and Exit 10 on Line 4. Our judgment: start in the late afternoon so you reach the museum before it closes at 18:00, or walk after dark, when the museum is shut but the wall and city are lit.

en.heading: Inwangsan and Namsan: pairing the wall with Seochon or the tower
paragraphs: Inwangsan, 339 meters, is a granite mountain of exposed rock formations with names such as Chimabawi (skirt rock), Seonbawi and Gichabawi (train rock). Its name is Buddhist, and like Baegak it was closed after the 1968 raid, reopening only in 1993. The section runs 4.0 kilometers from the site of Donuimun to Changuimun, takes about two and a half hours and is rated among the hardest. There are no toilets once you are on the mountain, and the city warns that the many rock sections need extra care in winter.

Inwangsan makes most sense from Seochon, the old neighborhood on its eastern slope, where our Seochon walk climbs from Suseongdong valley toward the ridge and ends at the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum by Changuimun. Because Changuimun is also where the Baegak section begins, strong walkers can join the two, 8.7 kilometers of steep ground in all. For most visitors one mountain a day is plenty.

Namsan is the long, moderate option, and the one most visitors meet by accident on the way to N Seoul Tower. The official section passes the National Theater, climbs wooden stairs to the summit with its beacon mound and Palgakjeong pavilion, and descends past the cable car station and the Jamdubong viewpoint toward Baekbeom Square. Our Namsangol and Namsan guide covers the climb from the hanok village and the ways down; it pairs well with an afternoon in Myeong-dong.

en.heading: Four summit photos and a certificate from the city
paragraphs: Seoul issues a free completion certificate to anyone who walks the full 18.6 kilometers, and the proof is four selfies. Take a photo of yourself, with your face clearly visible, at the four designated spots: the Cheongundae stone or the summit stone on Baegak, the Naksan Park sign or the Naksan viewpoint sign, the old beacon site on Namsan, and Satgatbawi or the summit sign on Inwangsan. Group photos do not count; each walker needs their own.

Upload the four photos with your details on the official site, seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr, then collect the certificate on the day you booked at either the Hanyangdoseong Ruins Exhibition Hall on Namsan or the Hyehwa-dong Exhibition and Information Center near Hyehwamun. Pickup runs Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 to 17:00, except 12:00 to 13:00, and both offices close on Mondays, January 1 and the days of Seollal and Chuseok. The application pages are in Korean, so a translation app helps.

Each person can receive one certificate per quarter, and the accompanying badge changes color with the season; complete all four seasons and the city adds a metal badge. Separately, a stamp tour at the four main gates issues its own badge at the stamp points. Our judgment: the certificate is a good excuse to see all four mountains over a trip, one section per day, rather than a reason to march the whole loop at once.

en.heading: Stairs, ice and no shops: walking the wall safely
paragraphs: The wall runs through the middle of a city of millions, which makes it easy to underestimate. The Baegak and Inwangsan sections have no convenience stores, and once you start either one there are no toilets for about two hours. The steps are steep, and the city singles out Inwangsan's rock sections for extra care in winter. Its own advice is practical: cushioned trail shoes, a small pack with water, snacks and a spare layer, gloves and a warm hat in winter, and crampons if snow has fallen.

Treat the wall itself as the heritage site it is. Do not climb onto it, write on it or push anything into the joints, and carry your rubbish out. Where the path is narrow or rocky, walk in single file, and in residential stretches such as Jangsu Village and Ihwa Village, keep your voice down. For help in English, the Seoul Global Center answers on 02-120 (press 9).
checklist: Use a toilet before you start Baegak or Inwangsan; there are none for about two hours.
Carry water and snacks: no shops on Baegak or Inwangsan.
Wear trail shoes with grip; add crampons after snow.
On Baegak, keep to the recommended hours: 09:00–17:00 from November to February.
Obey no-photography signs near military facilities on Baegak.
Do not climb on the wall; walk single file on narrow stretches.
Keep quiet in Jangsu Village, Ihwa Village and other residential lanes.

en.heading: A Baegak morning, from Changuimun down to Samcheong-dong
paragraphs: This half day suits a dry, clear morning outside the coldest weeks. At about 09:00, take green bus 7212, 1020 or 7022 from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 3 on Line 3 to the Jahamun Gogae (Yun Dong-ju Hill) stop, then walk two minutes to Changuimun, the northwest small gate. Use a toilet and buy water before you leave the road, since there are neither for about two hours on the mountain.

Climb the stairs past the Dolphin Rest Area to Baegangmaru, the 342-meter summit stone, which takes most of the first hour or more. Continue down past the 1968 pine and Cheongundae to the Baegak gokseong bastion for the widest view, then on to Sukjeongmun. To include the new southwest trail, branch off at the Dolphin Rest Area on the way up; it ends at the 1968 pine on the main route, so climb back up to Baegangmaru from there before heading east, and allow extra time.

From Sukjeongmun follow the wall to the Malbawi viewpoints, then take the branch signed for Samcheong Park, about a 20-minute descent. From the park it is about ten minutes on foot into Samcheong-dong for a late lunch, and the lanes of Bukchon lie just beyond. Allow three to four hours in all, including stops. On a winter day, start no earlier than the 09:00 recommended time and plan to be off the mountain well before 17:00.

faq.q: Do I still need ID or a permit to hike Bugaksan?
faq.a: No. The Seoul City Wall official site lists the Baegak (Bugaksan) section as open 24 hours a day, every day, on a self-entry basis, with no registration. It recommends walking within set hours, 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February. Photography is still restricted near military facilities, so follow the signs on the trail.

faq.q: Which section of the Seoul City Wall is best for beginners?
faq.a: Naksan. From Hyehwamun, near Hansung University Station, the path follows the wall gently downhill past Naksan Park and Ihwa Village to Heunginjimun in about an hour. It is the city's easiest-rated section, it is open around the clock, and it is known for sunset and night views.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk the whole wall?
faq.a: The four official sections add up to about ten and a half hours of walking over roughly 18.6 kilometers, plus time for stops and the flat stretches through the city. The city says it can be done in a day but recommends walking it in sections, which is also how most people earn the completion certificate.

faq.q: Is it safe to hike the city wall in winter?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Naksan and most of Namsan are paved or stepped and manageable. Baegak's long staircases and Inwangsan's rock sections freeze, and the city advises gloves, a hat and crampons after snow. Start after 09:00, carry water, and finish Baegak well before its recommended 17:00 winter cutoff.

faq.q: Is the Seoul City Wall a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: Not yet. It is part of a nomination called the Capital Fortifications of Hanyang, together with Bukhansanseong and Tangchundaeseong. The full dossier was scheduled for submission by February 1, 2026, with an ICOMOS evaluation mission expected between August and October 2026. Treat it as nominated until UNESCO announces a decision.

en.heading: Dry, bright and cold: what a Seoul winter is really like
paragraphs: Seoul's winter is better described as cold and dry than as snowy. In the Korea Meteorological Administration's climate normals for the city, January is the coldest month with an average of −1.9°C, and December, January and February together bring only 67.6 millimeters of precipitation, about 5 percent of the year's total. The air is driest in late winter, and the normal date of the first snow is November 20. Expect clear, sharp days with freezing mornings, and treat snow as a bonus rather than something to plan around.

The cold explains a great deal of traditional Korean life. Hanok were built around ondol (온돌), underfloor heating that warmed rooms from below, which is why people sat, ate and slept on the floor; the habit survives in heated restaurant floors and the hot stone rooms of bathhouses. Winter was also the season of stored food: kimchi made in late autumn, fermented soybean blocks hung to dry, and hot porridges and soups. Visiting now, you see the city as it was designed to be lived in, turned inward toward warm rooms.

The Korea Meteorological Administration issues a cold-wave advisory (한파주의보) between October and April when morning lows are expected to stay at −12°C or below for at least two days, or when they are forecast to fall 10°C or more from the previous day to 3°C or lower, at least 3°C below normal. On those days, keep outdoor sightseeing to the late morning and early afternoon, when the sun is highest, and have an indoor plan ready in the same district.

en.heading: Shorter palace days: the winter timetable
paragraphs: Palace hours follow the daylight, and the winter schedule catches out visitors who plan by summer habits. Gyeongbokgung (경복궁) closes at 17:00 from November to February, and the gates stop admitting visitors at 16:00, so a palace afternoon has to begin by about 14:00. Changdeokgung (창덕궁) and Jongmyo (종묘) close at 17:30 from November to January, then switch to their 18:00 spring closing in February, a month before Gyeongbokgung does.

Two palaces ignore the season. Deoksugung (덕수궁) and Changgyeonggung (창경궁) stay open until 21:00 all year, with last entry at 20:00, and the heritage service lists Deoksugung for regular night viewing. In winter that matters more than in summer: darkness falls early, so these two give you the most time among lit halls. Weekly closures never change with the season. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays; Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung on Mondays. When a closing day falls on a public holiday, the palace opens and closes on the next day that is not a holiday.

Our judgment on order: in December and January, book a Secret Garden session for the late morning and see Changdeokgung's halls around it, reach Gyeongbokgung by 14:00 on another day, and save Deoksugung or Changgyeonggung for the end of the afternoon, when everything else has shut. Jongmyo's wide, open stone courts offer no shelter from the wind, so choose a sunny midday; on Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays it is seen only on timed tours, with English tours at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00.

en.heading: Palaces and temples under snow
paragraphs: If snow falls overnight, go to a palace at 09:00 the next morning, before the courtyards are swept and trodden. Gyeongbokgung is the classic choice, because the white roofs of the throne-hall compound sit in front of Bugaksan, the granite mountain behind the palace, and the contrast is at its sharpest in early light. Look at the eaves as well as the halls: snow picks out the line of small guardian figures that run along the roof ridges.

The Secret Garden (후원) behind Changdeokgung changes most in winter. Bare branches open up views of pavilions that summer leaves hide, and the ponds may freeze. It is seen only on timed tours, and in December, January and February the English sessions run at 10:30, 11:30 and 14:30. Take the 11:30 slot for the warmest part of the day, and wear shoes with grip, because the garden paths climb and descend on earth and stone that can ice over.

Temples are calmer in winter and, for many visitors, more absorbing. Jogyesa in central Seoul and Bongeunsa across from COEX are at their quietest on cold weekday mornings, when a few worshippers come and go and the courtyards are almost empty. Keep the usual etiquette: side doors, shoes off, socks on, phone silent. If you want more than a walk-through, a one-day Templestay program suits the season better than an overnight stay with an early start; our temple guide explains the formats and how to book.

en.heading: Dressing for freezing streets and overheated rooms
paragraphs: The hardest part of a Seoul winter is not the cold itself but the constant switching between freezing streets and warm interiors. Subway cars, museums, teahouses and restaurants are heated, and some restaurants seat you on heated floors. Dress in layers you can take off quickly: a thermal base layer, a warm mid-layer and a windproof coat, plus gloves, a hat and a scarf that will fit in a bag. Lip balm and moisturizer help in the dry air.

Footwear matters more than visitors expect. Palace courtyards are paved with uneven stone and packed earth, temple steps are worn, and hillside lanes in neighborhoods such as Bukchon are steeper than they look when they freeze. Wear shoes with real grip, and if you plan a mountain walk on the city wall after snow, take crampons. Wearing hanbok in winter also works, provided you put thermal layers underneath and a coat on top; long hems pick up slush, so lift them on wet courtyards.

Indoors, a few habits keep things smooth. In restaurants, take your coat off and hang it on the back of your chair or put it in the bag or box the staff may offer, so it does not pick up the smell of the grill. Expect to remove your shoes in floor-seated teahouses and restaurants, so boots that lace slowly become a chore by the third stop; slip-on winter shoes with grip are the practical choice, with warm socks you are happy to show.

en.heading: Bungeoppang, hotteok and a cup of fish-cake broth
paragraphs: Cold weather brings out a set of street snacks that many Koreans associate with winter. Bungeoppang (붕어빵) is a fish-shaped pastry filled most often with sweet red-bean paste, though custard cream and chocolate versions also appear. Hotteok (호떡) is a chewy pancake pressed on a hot griddle around brown sugar, cinnamon and nuts; let it cool for a minute, because the melted sugar is far hotter than the crust. Gyeranppang (계란빵) is a small muffin-like bread baked with a whole egg on top.

The most warming snack costs very little: eomuk (어묵), skewers of fish cake kept in a simmering pot, sold with a paper cup of hot broth to drink. Roasted chestnuts (군밤, gunbam) and roasted sweet potatoes (군고구마, gungoguma) were once roasted on braziers on street corners and are now also sold in convenience stores and subway stations, and convenience stores add steamed buns and large dumplings for the winter months.

Carts come and go, so do not build a plan around one particular stall. Market food streets are the reliable option, and our street food guide explains where to eat, how to order and what to check if you avoid fish, pork or nuts. For a sit-down warm-up, order hot citron or ginger tea at a traditional teahouse in Insadong or Bukchon, and take your shoes off at the door if the room has a heated floor.

en.heading: The bathhouse answer to a freezing afternoon
paragraphs: Many Koreans spend a freezing weekend afternoon at a jjimjilbang (찜질방), a bathhouse that adds heated rooms, snack bars and mats to its baths, where people lie on warm floors for hours. It is the most Korean way to recover from a morning in the cold, and in midwinter it makes sense in a way it never quite does in July.

VisitKorea's advice for first-timers is to start in the gentler rooms, around 30 to 40°C, and to limit time in rooms above 60°C to about 20 minutes. Your locker key is usually worn on the wrist or ankle and is used to charge extras, which you pay for at the counter when you leave. The classic snack is a roasted egg with sikhye (식혜), a sweet rice drink. Drink water between rounds and skip alcohol beforehand. Our jjimjilbang guide walks through the entry routine, the bathing rules and the etiquette step by step.

en.heading: When the wind wins: museums that open long
paragraphs: Some days are simply too cold for courtyards, and Seoul's best answer is the National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관) in Yongsan. Its permanent galleries are free and open 9:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with last entry 30 minutes before closing. Note three winter closures: the exhibition halls shut for maintenance on the first Monday of December, which in 2026 is December 7, and the museum closes on January 1 and on Seollal day, February 7, 2027.

On the Gyeongbokgung grounds, the National Folk Museum of Korea (국립민속박물관) keeps winter hours of 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February, with last entry at 16:00, and it opens on Tuesdays when the palace does not. It is free, and its galleries on the Korean year explain the winter customs mentioned in this guide. It also closes on January 1 and on Seollal day. For more swaps by district, including covered markets, teahouses and Saturday performances, see our guide to indoor culture for rain, freezes and heat waves.

en.heading: Solstice porridge and the midnight bell
paragraphs: Around December 22 comes dongji (동지), the winter solstice and the longest night of the year, once called little New Year's Day. The custom is patjuk (팥죽), red-bean porridge with small rice-dough balls. Its red color was believed to drive away evil spirits, and families once offered bowls to household gods before eating. That rite is rarely practiced now, but patjuk is still widely eaten on the day, and a saying holds that you only grow a year older once you have had your bowl.

On New Year's Eve, Seoul rings in the year at Bosingak, the bell pavilion on Jongno. At the ceremony on December 31, 2025, the program ran from 22:50 to 00:20, with a countdown and 33 strikes of the bell at midnight. Roads around Jongno, Cheonggyebuk-ro and Ujeongguk-ro were closed from 18:00 on December 31 until 07:00 the next morning, and the last subway trains, along with buses passing the area, were extended to about 02:00. The city announces each year's arrangements in December. If you go, arrive early, dress for standing still in the cold, and plan your route home before midnight.

en.heading: Seollal 2027: what opens and what closes
paragraphs: Seollal (설날), the Lunar New Year, falls on Sunday, February 7, 2027, according to the Korea AeroSpace Administration's official almanac, and the public holiday runs from Saturday, February 6, to Tuesday, February 9, the last day being a substitute holiday. Many Seoul residents travel to family homes, so the city's sights grow quieter while trains and express buses fill. The holiday dish is tteokguk (떡국), sliced rice-cake soup, and the greeting is 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo), receive many New Year blessings.

The palaces stay open through the holiday, because a closing day that falls on a public holiday is moved to the next ordinary day. In 2027 that rule stacks every closure onto one date: Monday, February 8, and Tuesday, February 9, are both holidays, so Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo all close together on Wednesday, February 10. Museums are less generous: the National Museum of Korea and the National Folk Museum both close on Seollal day itself, February 7. Expect some family-run restaurants to close for the main days, and check opening status in your map app the evening before. Our Seollal and Chuseok guide covers transport and holiday programs.

en.heading: A winter Wednesday, hour by hour
paragraphs: This plan avoids the Monday and Tuesday palace closures and uses the National Museum's Wednesday late opening as a fallback. It suits any Wednesday from December to February except February 10, 2027, when every heritage-service palace is closed after Seollal. If snow fell overnight, keep the 09:00 palace start without fail; it is the best hour of the day. Walking between the stops is short except the subway ride to Deoksugung, and every outdoor stop has a heated indoor one within a few minutes.
checklist: 09:00 Gyeongbokgung at opening; walk the main axis while the light is low and the courtyards are quiet.
10:30 National Folk Museum on the palace grounds, free and open until 17:00 in winter.
12:00 Lunch: a hot soup or stew on a heated floor in Samcheong-dong or Insadong.
13:30 Jogyesa, then a traditional teahouse in Insadong for citron or ginger tea.
15:30 Street snacks from a cart if you find one: hotteok, bungeoppang or eomuk with broth.
16:30 Deoksugung as the light fades; stay for the lit halls after dark (last entry 20:00).
18:30 Dinner, then a jjimjilbang, or the National Museum of Korea until 21:00 if the wind is fierce.

faq.q: Are Seoul's palaces open in winter?
faq.a: Yes, all year, with shorter hours. Gyeongbokgung is open 09:00 to 17:00 from November to February, with last entry at 16:00. Changdeokgung and Jongmyo close at 17:30 from November to January. Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung stay open until 21:00 all year. Weekly closures are Tuesdays for Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo and Mondays for the others.

faq.q: Does it snow much in Seoul?
faq.a: Less than many visitors expect. Seoul's winters are cold and dry: December to February together average only 67.6 millimeters of precipitation, about 5 percent of the annual total, and the normal first-snow date is November 20. Snow does fall in Seoul, but plan for clear, freezing days and treat a snowy palace morning as luck.

faq.q: How cold is Seoul in January?
faq.a: January is the coldest month, with an average temperature of −1.9°C in the Korea Meteorological Administration's climate normals. Mornings are often well below freezing, and cold waves can push lows to −12°C or below; that is the threshold for a cold-wave advisory. Wind makes it feel colder, so pack gloves, a hat and layers.

faq.q: What is closed in Seoul over Seollal 2027?
faq.a: The palaces stay open from February 6 to 9, then Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo all close on Wednesday, February 10. The National Museum of Korea and the National Folk Museum close on Seollal day, February 7. Some family-run restaurants close for the main days, so check opening status the evening before.

faq.q: What warm street food should I try in Seoul in winter?
faq.a: Start with eomuk, fish-cake skewers sold with a cup of hot broth, then try bungeoppang, a fish-shaped pastry usually filled with red-bean paste, and hotteok, a griddled pancake filled with brown sugar, cinnamon and nuts. Roasted chestnuts and sweet potatoes are also sold in convenience stores and subway stations in winter.

title.en: Gyeonghuigung and the Seoul Museum of History: The Rebuilt West Palace

summary.en: Gyeonghuigung, Seoul's rebuilt west palace, and the free Seoul Museum of History next door: what survives, the five galleries, Donuimun's closure and a half-day plan.

guide.audience: Independent visitors around Gwanghwamun who want a quiet, free palace and a clear account of how Seoul grew, without wasting time on sites that are now closed.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Hours, closures and tour times can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: Give Gyeonghuigung about 45 minutes and the Seoul Museum of History two hours: both are free, both close on Mondays, and they stand side by side on Saemunan-ro. Nearly every palace building is a modern reconstruction, which is exactly what makes the visit instructive. Skip Donuimun Museum Village, which is fenced off, and walk on to Deoksugung instead.

en.heading: A west palace raised on a rumor of royal energy
paragraphs: Gyeonghuigung (경희궁) began with a prophecy. In 1617 King Gwanghaegun (광해군), who considered Changdeokgung an unlucky residence, was told by a geomancer that royal energy gathered over the house of his half-brother, Prince Jeongwon (정원군), and he ordered a palace built on the confiscated site. He never moved in. A coup deposed him in 1623 and put Prince Jeongwon's eldest son on the throne as King Injo (인조). Because the coup and the Yi Gwal rebellion that followed had burned Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung, Injo governed from the palace raised on his own father's land.

Until 1760 it was called Gyeongdeokgung (경덕궁); King Yeongjo (영조) renamed it because the old name sounded the same as the posthumous title of Injo's father. People also called it Seogwol (서궐), the West Palace, as the counterpart of Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung, known together as the East Palace. It was no hunting lodge. Encykorea counts about 1,500 kan (칸), the bays between columns by which Korean buildings are measured, and the museum counts more than 100 buildings. Ten kings from Injo to Cheoljong used it. Sukjong was born and died here, Yeongjo spent long stretches of his 52-year reign here, and Gyeongjong, Jeongjo and Heonjong were enthroned here.

Set your expectations before you go. Gyeonghuigung is the least complete of Seoul's five Joseon palaces, and apart from its main gate every hall you see was rebuilt after 1990. That is why it repays an hour: no other palace shows so plainly how a royal site was taken apart and partly pieced back together. If your trip has room for one palace, choose Gyeongbokgung or Changdeokgung. If you want quiet, free entry and a lesson in how heritage is lost, come here and pair it with the Seoul Museum of History (서울역사박물관) next door, which is the stronger half of the visit.

en.heading: How a 100-building palace became a schoolyard
paragraphs: The losses began well before colonial rule. A fire in 1829 burned about half the main halls, which were rebuilt the following year. Then, when King Gojong's (고종) court rebuilt Gyeongbokgung in the 1860s, everything at Gyeonghuigung except a few principal halls was pulled down and carried off as building material. Around 1902 the palace was still joined to Gyeongungung, today's Deoksugung, by an arched bridge over the road, and the museum's history page shows a photograph of it. Even so, the West Palace was largely empty by the time Japan took control of Korea.

Japan finished the job. In 1907 a middle school of the Japanese Residency-General was built inside the palace, and the builders cut down the high ground and filled the low ground, reshaping the site. The palace passed to the colonial government in 1910, and in 1915 the grounds became Gyeongseong Middle School (경성중학교), a school for Japanese residents. Through the 1920s and 1930s the remaining halls were sold or moved away, and more than 25,000 pyeong, about 8 hectares, of palace land was cut off for official housing of the colonial Monopoly Bureau. By 1945 the palace survived mainly as a place name.

Liberation did not bring it back. Seoul High School used the grounds and more land was sold. When the school moved south of the river to Seocho-gu in June 1980, Encykorea records, the site went to a private company. The state designated it Historic Site No. 271 that September, the city acquired the land from Hyundai Engineering & Construction in 1986 in an exchange, and excavations in 1985 and 1987 confirmed where the throne hall had stood. Rebuilding followed in stages through the 1990s, and the restored palace opened to the public in 2002.

en.heading: Where the palace buildings went
paragraphs: The most useful fact to carry in with you is that the original buildings were scattered across the city, and some still stand elsewhere. Knowing which is which turns a quiet walk into a small piece of detective work. The table follows the main ones, using the museum's building notes and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Encykorea), the Academy of Korean Studies' reference work.

Heunghwamun is the one major structure on the grounds that dates from the founding. Built around 1618, it originally stood farther east on Saemunan-ro, on the site of today's Salvation Army building, facing east. When it came home in 1988 that site was occupied, so it was set up where a lesser gate, Gaeyangmun (개양문), had been. It has a single story, unlike the two-story main gates of Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung, which Encykorea links to the palace's original role as a refuge for the king. Its name board was said to glow at night, giving the area the old name Yajugae (야주개).

en.heading: Reading the rebuilt halls, from goblin bridge to King Rock
paragraphs: Start at the stone bridge in front of the museum. Look for the goblin faces, dokkaebi (도깨비), carved between its arches and the stone beasts on its railings, placed to stop evil influences from entering the palace. Then pass through Sungjeongmun (숭정문) to Sungjeongjeon. The hall was rebuilt in 1991 on the spot the excavations confirmed, reusing foundation stones recovered from the ground, so parts of its platform are far older than the timber above. If the doors are open, look up: two dragons face each other in the coffered ceiling over the royal seat and its screen of the sun, moon and five peaks.

Behind it stand Jajeongjeon (자정전), the council hall where the king met ministers and held lectures, and Taeryeongjeon (태령전), which from 1744 housed a portrait of Yeongjo. Both were rebuilt from the Seogwol doan (서궐도안), an old drawing of the whole palace, and at Jajeongjeon the city left a patch of excavated floor bricks on the west side as it was found. Behind Taeryeongjeon rises Seoam (서암), a boulder with a spring inside it. Its original name, Wangam (왕암), King Rock, fed the story that drew Gwanghaegun here. Sukjong renamed it in 1708 and had the new name carved; that inscribed stone is now in the National Palace Museum.

Step back and notice the plan. Encykorea points out that Gyeonghuigung faced east and set its formal and residential courts side by side, with the main gate at a corner, unlike Gyeongbokgung's south-facing sequence of courts one behind another. The looser layout, which Changdeokgung shares, appears to have been a deliberate step down in formality for a secondary palace. It is a useful contrast to carry to Gyeongbokgung, where everything lines up on a single axis from the gate to the throne.

Gyeonghuigung is free and needs no ticket. It opens from 09:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:30, and closes on Mondays and January 1. The museum asks visitors not to bring coffee, drinks or snacks onto the palace grounds. Free commentary walks by two volunteer heritage groups are listed on the museum's Korean page for Fridays at 14:00 and 15:00, Saturdays at 13:00, 14:00 and 15:00, and Sundays every half hour from 13:00 to 15:00. The listing names no English sessions, so plan to explore the halls on your own with the notes above.

en.heading: The Seoul Museum of History: Hanyang to megacity in five zones
paragraphs: The Seoul Museum of History stands beside the palace on land the city acquired in 1986 partly in order to build a municipal museum, and its permanent galleries fill the third floor in five zones arranged by date. Zone 1 covers the Joseon capital from 1392 to 1863: how Hanyang was laid out by geomantic and Confucian principles, how the wars of 1592 and 1636 left it in ashes, how it grew into a commercial city in the late eighteenth century, and how its neighborhoods, from Bukchon to the villages outside the wall, differed in character.

Zone 2 runs from the opening of the ports to 1910 and includes a section titled The New Heart of Seoul, Jeong-dong, about the neighborhood around Deoksugung. Zone 3 covers Gyeongseong (경성), as the colonial administration called the city, from 1910 to 1945, setting resistance and the independence movement beside the modern city that grew up at the same time. Zone 4 follows the capital of the Republic from liberation and war through the 1970s push south of the river to the 2002 World Cup. Zone 5 ends at a 1:1,500 scale model of present-day Seoul in a panoramic theater.

Spend your time where the palace leaves off. Zone 1 explains the city Gyeonghuigung belonged to, and its section on Seongjeosimni (성저십리), the belt of about 4 kilometers outside the wall, holds the museum's most surprising fact: by late Joseon roughly half the capital's residents lived outside the walls, around river ports such as Mapo and Yongsan. Move faster through Zone 4 if you know modern Korean history, and finish at the model, which joins the districts you have been crossing by subway into one landscape of rivers and ridges.

Admission is free. Regular hours are 09:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:30, and Fridays run to 21:00. From September 15 to November 30, 2026, an autumn late opening keeps the museum open until 21:00, last entry 20:30, on every open day except Thursday. It closes on Mondays and January 1 but opens when a Monday is a public holiday. Free English tours of the permanent galleries start on Thursdays at 11:00 and 14:00, Fridays at 14:00 and Saturdays at 11:00; you simply join at the museum, and times can change. An English audio guide is lent free at the first-floor information desk against an ID, so bring your passport.

en.heading: Donuimun Museum Village is closed, so skip older itineraries
paragraphs: Many guides still send you a few minutes west to Donuimun Museum Village (돈의문박물관마을), a block of older houses and former restaurants that the city opened in 2017 and relaunched in 2019 as a so-called living museum of about 40 small exhibition and experience spaces. Do not plan on it. Seoul decided in 2024 to clear the village for a park, operations ended in 2025, and when Munhwa Ilbo reporters visited at the end of April 2026, a wooden fence blocked the entrance and a single business, which had lost its eviction case, was still trading.

The Donuimun History Museum (돈의문역사관), a branch of the Seoul Museum of History inside the village, closed on September 1, 2025 for the same greening and redesign project, and the museum's notice gives December 31, 2026 as the end of the closure. That is a real loss for anyone interested in the palace, because the branch held some of the clearest evidence of how far Gyeonghuigung once reached: excavated remains of the palace wall, viewed from a deck, in what had become an ordinary residential block. Check the branch page before counting on it in 2027.

The practical result is simple: your walk west from the palace now ends at a fence, and the better onward route runs the other way, into Jeong-dong. The city wall's west gate, Donuimun (돈의문), which gave the village its name, no longer stands either, so the old relationship between palace, wall and gate now survives mainly on paper. If that geography interests you, linger in the museum's Zone 1, which is organized around Hanyang's districts inside the wall and the villages beyond it.

en.heading: A four-hour plan, palace first
paragraphs: This plan starts at 10:00 on a Thursday or Saturday so you can join the 11:00 English tour; on Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday or Sunday, use the audio guide instead and keep the same order. It avoids Mondays, when the palace, the museum and Deoksugung are all closed, and it ends with a walk to Deoksugung, which stays open until 21:00 with last entry at 20:00, so the afternoon is yours to stretch. Allow an extra hour if you read every panel.
checklist: 10:00 Enter Gyeonghuigung through Heunghwamun from Saemunan-ro; Gwanghwamun Station (Line 5) Exits 6–8 are about seven minutes away on foot.
10:05 Geumcheongyo bridge and its goblin faces, then Sungjeongmun and Sungjeongjeon: the platform stones and, if the doors are open, the dragon ceiling (20 minutes).
10:25 Jajeongjeon, Taeryeongjeon and the Seoam boulder behind it (20 minutes).
10:50 Seoul Museum of History: leave bags at the storage by the entrance, borrow an audio guide with your passport if you are not taking the tour, and go up to the third floor.
11:00 English tour of the permanent galleries on Thursday or Saturday, or Zones 1 and 2 on your own (about an hour).
12:15 Zones 3 to 5, ending at the scale model of Seoul (40 minutes).
13:00 A light lunch at the museum café, or a restaurant along Saemunan-ro.
14:00 Walk to Deoksugung through Jeong-dong, as described below.

en.heading: Adding Deoksugung and Jeong-dong without backtracking
paragraphs: Gyeonghuigung and Deoksugung belong to the same story. Around 1902 the arched bridge mentioned above linked them across the road, and Zone 2 of the museum devotes a section to Jeong-dong, the neighborhood around Deoksugung where foreign legations, mission schools and churches gathered in the late nineteenth century. Walking from one to the other puts those panels on the ground. Walk west along Saemunan-ro to the old site of Donuimun in front of Kangbuk Samsung Hospital, turn toward the Kyunghyang Shinmun newspaper building, and you are on Jeongdong-gil (정동길), which runs east past Ewha Girls' High School and Jeongdong First Methodist Church to Deoksugung's Daehanmun gate. For scale, the museum puts City Hall Station, beside Deoksugung, about 15 minutes away on foot.

Deoksugung opens from 09:00 to 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, and closes on Mondays. The pairing works because the two palaces are opposites: one rebuilt from almost nothing, the other the seat of the short-lived Korean Empire, with Western-style stone halls built in the same years the museum's Zone 2 describes. Jungmyeongjeon (중명전), a Deoksugung building off Jeongdong-gil, keeps shorter hours, 09:30 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00, so stop there first if you are walking in the afternoon. Our five-palaces comparison covers Deoksugung's fees and free days.

If you arrive in the afternoon instead, reverse the order sensibly rather than completely. Do the museum first, because its galleries outlast the palace on Fridays and during the autumn late opening, then the palace before its 17:30 last entry, and keep Deoksugung for the evening. On a Monday none of this works, since Gyeonghuigung, the museum and Deoksugung are all shut; make that a Gyeongbokgung day and come back on another.

faq.q: Is Gyeonghuigung worth visiting if I have already seen Gyeongbokgung?
faq.a: Yes, if you have an hour and an interest in how heritage is lost and rebuilt. It is quiet and free, and nearly every hall is a reconstruction on excavated foundations, which makes the history easy to read. It is not a substitute for Gyeongbokgung or Changdeokgung on a first trip with time for one palace.

faq.q: Do I need tickets for Gyeonghuigung or the Seoul Museum of History?
faq.a: No. Both are free and neither issues tickets for general entry. The museum's English tours of the permanent galleries also need no booking: join at the museum on Thursdays at 11:00 and 14:00, Fridays at 14:00 or Saturdays at 11:00.

faq.q: Is Donuimun Museum Village open?
faq.a: No. Seoul decided in 2024 to turn the village into green space, operations ended in 2025, and in late April 2026 its entrance was fenced off. The Donuimun History Museum inside it has been closed since September 1, 2025, with the museum's notice giving December 31, 2026 as the end of the closure.

faq.q: Is the Seoul Museum of History open on Mondays?
faq.a: Normally no; it closes every Monday and on January 1. When a Monday is a public holiday, the museum opens. Gyeonghuigung's own page lists Mondays as closing days without that exception, so on a holiday Monday plan on the museum only, or call 02-724-0274 first.

faq.q: How long does a visit to both take?
faq.a: About three hours: 45 minutes in the palace, two hours in the museum's five galleries including the scale model, and a short break. Add about 20 minutes for the walk on through Jeong-dong to Deoksugung, which is open until 21:00 except on Mondays.

en.heading: Five crafts, five very different hours
paragraphs: Korean craft was once a state enterprise. The Joseon legal code, the Gyeongguk daejeon (경국대전), assigned 2,841 artisans in 129 specialties to central government offices and 3,656 in 27 specialties to provincial ones, each making to fixed standards for diplomacy, the army, royal ritual and daily use. That division into narrow specialties survives in how crafts are taught today: one teacher, one material, one technique. Choosing a workshop therefore starts with choosing the material, because a knot, a shell inlay and a pot make for very different hours.

Who should do this? Travelers with an unhurried morning, a liking for close work and an interest in objects rather than sights. Skip it if you have only two days in Seoul, or if your idea of a souvenir is something to buy rather than make; the shops of Insadong will serve you better. The table compares the crafts that official Seoul listings currently offer to walk-in visitors or by booking, with an honest note on what survives the trip home.
