en.heading: Look before you make: the Seoul Museum of Craft Art
paragraphs: The Seoul Museum of Craft Art (서울공예박물관) opened in July 2021 as Korea's first public craft museum, in five remodeled buildings of the former Pungmun Girls' High School in Anguk-dong. The ground itself belongs to the story. It held the house of Prince Yeongeung, a son of King Sejong, and later Andong Byeolgung (안동별궁), a royal residence built for the wedding of the future King Sunjong, and the neighborhood was where the capital's government artisans, the gyeonggongjang (경공장), worked.

Before any class, see the permanent galleries that match your craft. On the second floor of Exhibition Building 2, From Nature to Craft traces how ore became metalwork, clay became earthenware and then ceramics, and wood and abalone shell became najeon lacquerware. Exhibition Building 1 follows artisans from the Joseon workshops through the industrial souvenirs of the colonial period. Exhibition Building 3 holds embroidery on its second floor, a permanent display since December 20, 2025, and bojagi (보자기), the patchwork wrapping cloths, on its third. Ten minutes with the bojagi will change how you judge any fabric object you buy later.

Admission is free, though rented exhibitions may charge. The galleries open from 10:00 to 18:00, with last entry 30 minutes before closing, and the museum closes on Mondays, except when a Monday is a public holiday, and on January 1. Anguk Station (Line 3) Exit 1 is about 60 meters away. Food and drink are not allowed inside, and the children's museum in the education building admits only visitors with an online reservation. Seasonal late openings, when the city runs them, are announced on the museum's visit page.

The museum also teaches, but its classes are built for residents. In 2026 it ran a free 90-minute evening class for adults on Tuesdays through November 24, in which 20 participants a session studied museum najeon, tried three shell techniques and made a small inlaid box. Places were released month by month on Seoul's public reservation site and went first come, first served. Watch the program page if you are staying for weeks; for a short trip, treat the museum as the looking half of the day.

en.heading: Maedeup: what a knot did on a Joseon costume
paragraphs: Maedeup (매듭) is far more than tying knots. Encykorea describes the full craft as twisting silk threads into yarn, dyeing it, braiding it into cord, tying the cord into set shapes and finishing it with tassels, sul (술). Under Joseon the royal clothing office, the Sangeuiwon (상의원), employed separate masters for cord-making and for knotting. Round cord, dong-dahoe (동다회), was used for knots and robe ties, while flat cord, nap-dahoe (납다회), was woven with patterns and worn as a belt. Knots first decorated ceremonial tassel hangings and later shrank into personal ornaments such as the norigae (노리개) that hangs from a woman's jacket tie.

The knots have names worth learning before a class: dorae (도래), the small button knot; yeonbong (연봉), the lotus bud; dongsimgyeol (동심결), the concentric-hearts knot; and butterfly, bee and dragonfly knots named for the shapes they make. The state designated maedeup-making national intangible heritage in 1968, and certified masters still carry it on. When you look at a norigae in a museum case, count the stages: cord, knot body and tassel could each be the work of a different specialist.

In a visitor session you will learn one or two knots, worked into something small such as the ring-knot garakji (가락지) bracelet or a silk daenggi key ring at the Bukchon center. It is the most portable of the crafts and the easiest to follow without Korean, because the teacher's hands show every step. Judge quality the same way when buying: even, firm knots with symmetrical loops, a tassel that hangs straight without frizz, and cord that is silk rather than shiny synthetic, which a good teacher or seller will tell you without being asked.

en.heading: Najeon: abalone shell, lacquer and two ways to cut
paragraphs: Najeon (나전) is the craft of grinding abalone or other shell, cutting it into patterns and fixing it to wood with lacquer. The Korea Heritage Service describes the sequence: a carpenter builds the wooden base, called baekgol (백골), which is smoothed and filled; shell is inlaid; then the surface is ground, lacquered and polished in repeated stages. The materials that matter most are the sap of the lacquer tree and the shell itself, mostly abalone, turban shell and pearl oyster, with the finest from Korea's south coast and the waters around Jeju. Tongyeong is the best-known najeon town and Wonju a center of lacquer.

Two cutting techniques define the look. In kkeuneumjil (끊음질), shell is cut into thread-thin strips called sangsa (상사) and laid down to build geometric patterns. In jureumjil (줄음질), thinned shell is cut with a fretsaw into motifs such as chrysanthemums, bamboo and turtles. Designs changed over time: peonies, chrysanthemums and lotuses in Goryeo and early Joseon, then birds and flowers, cranes, grapes and the Four Gentlemen plants by mid-Joseon. Once you know the two techniques, any box in a museum case tells you which hand made it.

Be realistic about what an hour can teach. The full process involves many cycles of lacquering and polishing, so a visitor session concentrates on the decorative step: arranging and fixing shell on a small mirror, coaster or box. The museum's 2026 class fitted three techniques, jureumjil, kkeuneumjil and halpae (할패), cracking shell into fragments, into 90 minutes, which gives a sense of the compression. When buying, tilt the piece: real shell flashes different colors as the angle changes, while printed or plastic imitations stay flat. Ask whether the finish is true lacquer, ottchil (옻칠), or a synthetic coating.

en.heading: Hanji, clay and safflower red
paragraphs: Hanji (한지), paper made from the inner bark of the paper mulberry, is taught at the Bukchon center by its own instructors, and our Insadong guide covers how to tell handmade sheets from printed imitations. One studio puts hanji to an unexpected use. At the Saeksil Munyang Nubi Workshop (색실문양누비공방), in a city-owned hanok, Kim Yun-seon runs classes in saeksil nubi, a quilting style that sews hanji cord, rather than cotton wadding, between layers of cloth in colored thread. The city lists a 50-minute single-row quilting session at 15,000 won and a mobile-making session of 30 to 40 minutes at 9,000 won, from 10:00 to 17:00.

Ceramics need a different plan. The Bukchon center offers an electric potter's wheel and, since 2026, a ceramic-repair session. A pot thrown on the wheel must dry and be fired before it is usable, which takes longer than most trips, so ask before you pay whether the studio fires work and how you would collect it; if you leave Seoul within days, choose repair or another craft you finish on the spot. To see what the masters achieved, the celadon and buncheong rooms at the National Museum of Korea are the best preparation.

The most striking color comes from a flower. The Traditional Hongyeom Workshop (전통홍염공방) belongs to Kim Gyeong-yeol, holder of Seoul's intangible heritage title for hongyeom (홍염), red dyeing with safflower. In Joseon, both the royal clothing office and the court supply office kept ten safflower dyers, and the deep red they produced colored the king's dragon robe. Visitors can see restored pieces and hear the process explained; dyeing with a range of natural dyestuffs is possible by advance booking. It opens from 10:00 to 17:00, about eight minutes on foot from Anguk Station Exit 2.

en.heading: How Bukchon's public craft hanok actually works
paragraphs: The Bukchon Traditional Craft Experience Center (북촌전통공예체험관), at 24-5 Bukchon-ro 12-gil, is a hanok owned by the city where artisans from Bukchon run short sessions in rotation. From May 2026, Jongno-gu expanded the roster to 46 programs led by 16 local workshops, organized by day of the week. The list includes a patchwork bracelet, a hopae (호패), the identity tag men carried in Joseon, a coaster with dancheong (단청) patterns, the painted decoration of palace and temple eaves, mother-of-pearl accessories, the potter's wheel, a silk daenggi key ring and a knot bracelet, plus new sessions on the gat (갓) hat key ring, loom weaving and ceramic repair.

Entry is free and sessions cost 5,000 to 15,000 won. The center opens from 10:00 to 17:00 from November to February and until 18:00 in the warmer months, and closes only on the days of Seollal and Chuseok, so it is one of the few craft options open on a Monday. Booking is the awkward part. The city's hanok portal says no reservation is needed, while Jongno-gu's 2026 announcement says places are taken first come, first served on yeyak.seoul.go.kr, Seoul's public reservation site, which requires a city account verified through a Korean mobile phone on first use.

For most short-term visitors that leaves two routes. If someone with a Korean phone can book for you, use the reservation site and pick your craft and weekday together, since each program runs only on certain days. Otherwise, arrive at opening on a weekday, ask which sessions have space and be ready to take whatever craft is running. The listings make no promise of English, so the visual crafts, knots and shell inlay, are the safest choices. The center is about 670 meters from Anguk Station Exit 2, through lanes where people live, so keep voices low.

en.heading: Six questions to ask before you pay
paragraphs: Private studios across Insadong, Bukchon and Seongsu sell craft classes online, and their quality runs from master workshops to assembly tables with a glue gun. The public venues above are a safe baseline, but the same questions sort any class quickly. Ask them by message before you book, or at the door with a translation app; a studio that answers clearly and specifically is usually one that teaches well, and a vague answer about materials is the clearest warning sign you will get.
checklist: Who teaches? Ask whether the instructor makes this craft professionally and holds a heritage title or trained under a holder; serious artisans say so readily.
What is the material? Silk or synthetic cord, real shell or printed film, true lacquer (옻칠, ottchil) or synthetic coating, handmade or machine hanji.
Which steps will you do yourself, and which arrive pre-made?
How long is the session and how many people share one teacher?
Can you take the piece away today, or does it need drying, curing or firing?
What does the fee include: materials, a box or bag for carrying, any tax?

en.heading: A craft morning around Anguk, with a Monday fallback
paragraphs: On any day from Tuesday to Sunday, start at the Seoul Museum of Craft Art at 10:00. Give 45 minutes to From Nature to Craft in Exhibition Building 2 and the najeon cases, then 20 minutes to the bojagi upstairs in Exhibition Building 3. Leave by 11:15 and walk north through Bukchon to the craft center, aiming to arrive before the late-morning sessions fill. Spend an hour on one craft, ideally the one you just studied in the galleries, and break for lunch in the lanes around Anguk Station or Samcheong-dong.

Spend the afternoon looking at what professionals sell. Insadong begins just south of Anguk Station, and its specialist hanji and brush shops are where the questions you asked in class become useful; our Insadong guide shows which kinds of shop to trust. If natural dye is your interest, contact the Traditional Hongyeom Workshop ahead of time and fit the dyeing session in after lunch instead, because it is a short walk from the same station.

On a Monday the museum is closed unless it is a public holiday, but the Bukchon center still runs its sessions, so reverse the day: craft in the morning, Insadong in the afternoon, and the museum on another day if your trip allows. Pack finished pieces flat in your hand luggage. Wrap shell-inlaid objects in clothing to protect lacquered corners and edges, roll paper rather than folding it, and wash naturally dyed cloth alone in cold water for the first few washes.

faq.q: Do I need to speak Korean to take a craft class in Seoul?
faq.a: Not strictly, but expect Korean instruction. None of the official listings for the Seoul Museum of Craft Art or the Bukchon Traditional Craft Experience Center promises English sessions. Choose visual crafts such as maedeup knots or shell inlay, where you can follow the teacher's hands, and keep a translation app open for questions about materials and drying times.

faq.q: Can I book the Bukchon Traditional Craft Experience Center without a Korean phone number?
faq.a: Online booking runs through yeyak.seoul.go.kr, which asks first-time users to create a Seoul account verified through a Korean mobile phone. Without one, arrive at opening on a weekday and ask which sessions have space; the city's hanok portal says reservations are not required, though places can fill. You can also call 02-741-2148, in Korean.

faq.q: Is the Seoul Museum of Craft Art free?
faq.a: Yes. Admission to the museum is free, though rented exhibitions may charge. It opens from 10:00 to 18:00, with last entry 30 minutes before closing, and closes on Mondays (except public-holiday Mondays) and on January 1. It is about 60 meters from Anguk Station Exit 1 on Line 3.

faq.q: Can I take a pot home the same day after a wheel class?
faq.a: Usually not. A pot thrown on the wheel has to dry and be fired before it can be used, which takes longer than most visits. Ask before paying whether the studio fires and stores work and how you would collect it. If you are leaving soon, choose a ceramic-repair session or a craft you finish on the spot.

faq.q: How do I tell real mother-of-pearl from an imitation?
faq.a: Tilt the piece under light. Real shell flashes changing colors as the angle shifts and shows natural irregularity from piece to piece, while printed film or plastic looks uniform and flat. Ask whether the finish is true lacquer, ottchil (옻칠), and who made the piece; a seller of genuine najeon can answer both questions.

summary.en: Which Seoul art museum suits which Korean art: Leeum's free traditional galleries, MMCA Seoul, SeMA's Chun Kyung-ja room and the national museum, with hours and pairings.

guide.audience: Independent visitors who want to see Korean art in Seoul, traditional or modern, and need to choose between the major museums and fit one around a palace day.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Exhibitions, hours and fees change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: For traditional Korean art, go to Leeum, whose traditional galleries are free with a timed ticket, or the National Museum of Korea, where several painting and Buddhist art rooms are closed until January 28, 2027. For modern and contemporary art, MMCA Seoul beside Gyeongbokgung is open every day and free on Wednesday and Saturday evenings, and SeMA by Deoksugung is free and holds Chun Kyung-ja's paintings.

en.heading: Old Korean art or new: choose by the century
paragraphs: Seoul's art museums divide cleanly by period, and choosing the wrong one is the commonest way to waste an afternoon. Celadon, white porcelain, ink painting and Buddhist art belong to the National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관) and Leeum (리움미술관). Korean art since the early twentieth century belongs to the national Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, MMCA (국립현대미술관), and the city-run Seoul Museum of Art, SeMA (서울시립미술관). The contemporary museums run rotating exhibitions, so in a given month they may show more international work than Korean.

With one afternoon and an interest in Korea's classical arts, choose Leeum: its traditional galleries are free, compact and beautifully lit, and they are not affected by the national museum's current gallery closures. With an interest in living artists, choose MMCA Seoul, which stands beside Gyeongbokgung and opens every day. Add SeMA if you are already near Deoksugung, mainly for its permanent room of paintings by Chun Kyung-ja (천경자). If museums tire you quickly, pick one, see it well and spend the rest of the day at a palace.

Money is rarely the obstacle. The national museum's permanent galleries, Leeum's traditional galleries and SeMA's main collection displays cost nothing, and MMCA's paid exhibitions become free on Wednesday and Saturday evenings. Days matter more. Leeum, SeMA and MMCA's Deoksugung branch close on Mondays, Gyeongbokgung closes on Tuesdays, and the national museum shuts its galleries on the first Monday of March, June, September and December, which in 2026 falls on December 7.

A handful of Korean label words will carry you through any of these museums, and they double as search terms in map apps and museum shops. Cheongja (청자) is celadon, the green-glazed stoneware of Goryeo; buncheong (분청) is the slip-decorated stoneware of early Joseon; baekja (백자) is white porcelain. Seohwa (서화) means calligraphy and painting together, and on scrolls you will meet sansuhwa (산수화), landscape painting. In the modern museums, hanguk-hwa (한국화) marks painting in Korean ink and color traditions, as opposed to seoyang-hwa (서양화), Western-style painting in oil.

en.heading: Leeum: free traditional galleries in a terracotta tower
paragraphs: Leeum opened in 2004 in Hannam-dong, on the slopes of Namsan overlooking the Han River, as the museum of the Samsung Foundation of Culture, founded in 1965. Three architects shaped it. Mario Botta built Museum 1 in terracotta brick, meant to evoke the earth and fire of Korean ceramics; Jean Nouvel built Museum 2 for modern art in corroded stainless steel and glass; and Rem Koolhaas added a black-concrete box for the children's education center. A 2021 renovation reworked the lobby and the museum's identity. The museum frames itself as a place where traditional, contemporary and international art sit side by side.

For a visitor, the key fact is the price list. The traditional art permanent exhibition, 고미술 상설전 (gomisul sangseoljeon), and the Gabriel Orozco Garden are free; special exhibitions are paid, and on the last Wednesday of each month they are half price. Leeum's traditional galleries reward slow looking more than any checklist: choose a single case of ceramics and compare glazes, then do the same with a painting before moving on. If you have seen the national museum's ceramic rooms, Leeum is the natural second helping rather than a repeat.

Leeum opens from Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, with the ticket desk closing at 17:30, and closes on Mondays, January 1 and the days of Seollal and Chuseok. Online booking opens 14 days ahead, up to four tickets per person; you can also get tickets on the day, but the museum warns of waits when it is busy. Arrive any time from 20 minutes before your slot. A free digital guide is lent against ID, so carry your passport, and bags bigger than a backpack go in lockers. Outside guides may not lecture in the galleries. From Hangangjin Station (Line 6) Exit 1, walk 100 meters toward Itaewon, turn right at the first lane and climb for about five minutes.

en.heading: The National Museum's painting and ceramic rooms, with the 2026–27 closures
paragraphs: The National Museum of Korea holds the national collection of Korean painting, calligraphy, Buddhist art and ceramics, but until January 28, 2027 part of it is off view. A notice from the museum closes Calligraphy and Painting Rooms 202-3 and 202-4 from August 10, 2026, and Buddhist Painting (Room 203), Wood and Lacquer Crafts (204), Buddhist Sculpture (301), Metal Crafts (302) and the Room of Senses from July 6, 2026; all reopen on January 29, 2027. Rooms 202-1 and 202-2 and the third-floor ceramic rooms, Celadon (303) and Buncheong Ware and White Porcelain (304), are not on the closure list.

The permanent galleries are free and open from 9:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with entry ending 30 minutes before closing. The museum closes on January 1, Seollal and Chuseok, and shuts its galleries for maintenance on the first Monday of March, June, September and December, while the outdoor area stays open; the next of those days is December 7, 2026. For Korean art this winter, pair the open ceramic and painting rooms with Leeum, which lies in the same district; our National Museum guide sets out a three-hour route.

Which of the two should come first? The national museum gives breadth: a dynastic sequence that explains where each style sits, at the price of long corridors. Leeum gives concentration: fewer, carefully chosen works in a building designed around them. If you are new to Korean art, start with the national museum's ceramic rooms for context and finish at Leeum, where the pieces you now recognize can be looked at slowly. If time allows only one, choose Leeum this winter, while parts of the national museum are closed.

en.heading: MMCA Seoul: the national museum of the present, next to Gyeongbokgung
paragraphs: MMCA Seoul (국립현대미술관 서울관) occupies a block across the road from Gyeongbokgung's east side, on the edge of Bukchon, with the ridge of Bugaksan rising behind its courtyard. It is one of four MMCA museum sites, and its galleries are given over to changing exhibitions rather than a fixed display. In late 2026 its English tours cover an exhibition of the Korean artist Do Ho Suh; the free 40-minute tours start on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays at 13:30 and 14:30 at the entrance to Gallery 3, first come, first served, for up to 15 people.

Its hours are the most generous in the city: 10:00 to 18:00 every day, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, closed only on January 1 and the days of Seollal and Chuseok. That makes it the best art option on a Monday, when Leeum and SeMA are shut. Each paid exhibition has its own ticket, and an all-pass costs 10,000 won when three or more paid shows are running. Admission is free on Wednesday and Saturday evenings from 18:00 to 21:00 and on the last Wednesday of each month, and visitors under 24 or over 65 enter free with ID.

Use those free evenings deliberately. Gyeongbokgung closes at 17:00 from November to February, with last entry at 16:00, and it closes on Tuesdays, so on a Wednesday or Saturday leave the palace at closing, take an early dinner in Samcheong-dong or Bukchon, and walk into MMCA when the free late opening begins at 18:00. Take Line 3 to Anguk Station Exit 1 or Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 4, or Line 5 to Gwanghwamun Station Exit 2. An audio guide is available for a fee, and the museum's exhibition app is free.

en.heading: MMCA Deoksugung: modern Korean art inside the palace walls
paragraphs: MMCA's smallest Seoul site sits inside Deoksugung, and the museum describes it simply as a modern and contemporary art museum in a palace. It works best as part of a palace visit rather than a destination: its galleries are small, its exhibitions change through the year, and between shows there may be nothing to see. Check its page before you pay the palace fee, which MMCA's ticket does not include, and treat a good show there as a bonus to Deoksugung's own halls.

It opens Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and closes on Mondays and January 1. Exhibition fees vary, but the Wednesday and Saturday evening hours from 18:00 are free, as is the last Wednesday of the month. The catch is the palace gate: Deoksugung's main entrance, Daehanmun, stops admitting visitors at 20:00, so arrive before then. Deoksugung itself is open from 09:00 to 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, and closes on Mondays. The nearest stop is City Hall Station Exit 1, on Lines 1 and 2.

en.heading: SeMA: Chun Kyung-ja's paintings behind a courthouse facade
paragraphs: The Seoul Museum of Art's main building, Seosomun (서소문본관), at 61 Deoksugung-gil, wears the Renaissance-style front of a court built in 1928 under Japanese rule on the site of Pyeongriwon, Korea's first modern court. After liberation it housed the Supreme Court until 1995, and since 2002 a modern gallery building has stood behind the preserved facade. Admission is free except for special exhibitions, which makes it easy to slot into a walk along the Deoksugung stone-wall road.

Come for Chun Kyung-ja (천경자, 1924–2015), one of the defining painters of modern Korean color painting, who stayed committed to color painting while breaking with formal traditionalism to create a style of her own. In 1998 she gave 93 works she had kept, from the 1940s to the 1990s, to the city so the collection would never be dispersed. A permanent room on the second floor shows about 30 of them, many from her travels, in a centenary display whose title, roughly Toward the Wind That Moves the Soul, comes from her 1986 travel essay. The museum's free docent app provides commentary when no guide is on duty.

Seosomun opens from 10:00 to 20:00 Tuesday to Thursday and until 21:00 on Fridays; on weekends and public holidays it closes at 18:00 from November to February and at 19:00 from March to October. Entry ends an hour before closing. It closes on Mondays, except public-holiday Mondays, and on January 1. Use City Hall Station Exit 10 on Line 2, about 260 meters away, or Exit 1 on Line 1.

SeMA runs a network of branches, and one suits visitors interested in Korean art in particular. The Nam-Seoul Museum of Art (남서울미술관) occupies the former Belgian consulate, built in 1905 in Hoehyeon-dong and moved to Namhyeon-dong in 1983, and since 2023 its ground floor has displayed the sculpture of Kwon Jin-kyu (권진규), a pioneer of modern Korean sculpture. It is free, open from 10:00 to 20:00 on weekdays except Monday and 10:00 to 18:00 at weekends, a minute from Sadang Station Exit 6 on Line 2.

en.heading: Pairing art with palaces, day by day
paragraphs: Let the closing days decide the pairings. On a Monday, combine Gyeongbokgung, which is open that day, with MMCA Seoul across the road; Leeum, SeMA and Deoksugung are all shut. On a Tuesday, Gyeongbokgung is closed, so give the day to Leeum in the morning and the national museum in the afternoon; they lie in the same district, and the subway trip from Hangangjin to Ichon takes one change at Samgakji. From Wednesday to Sunday everything is open, and the evenings come into play.

A traditional-art Tuesday might run like this. Book Leeum for 10:00 and give it 90 minutes, then have lunch in Hannam-dong or Itaewon. Ride from Hangangjin to Ichon with the change at Samgakji and spend the afternoon in the national museum's ceramic rooms and open painting rooms, leaving by 17:30. Move the same plan to a Wednesday or Saturday and you can stay at the national museum until 21:00, since both museums are open that day.

Wednesday is the strongest evening of the week, because MMCA is free after 18:00 at both of its Seoul sites, Deoksugung stays open until 21:00 and SeMA until 20:00. The plan below keeps the walking to a few hundred meters around City Hall; on a Saturday the same order works if you visit SeMA earlier, since it closes at 18:00 on winter weekends. Pick MMCA Seoul instead if its exhibition interests you more than the one at Deoksugung.
checklist: 16:00 SeMA Seosomun from City Hall Station Exit 10: the Chun Kyung-ja room on the second floor (45 minutes).
17:00 Walk the Deoksugung stone-wall road to Daehanmun and enter the palace well before the 20:00 entry cut-off.
17:15 Deoksugung's halls in the last light, then a break.
18:00 MMCA Deoksugung, free from 18:00 on Wednesdays, if an exhibition is running (about an hour).
19:15 The palace grounds after dark until closing at 21:00.

faq.q: Which Seoul museum is best for traditional Korean art right now?
faq.a: Leeum, whose traditional galleries are free and unaffected by the national museum's closures, followed by the National Museum of Korea's open painting and ceramic rooms (202-1, 202-2, 303 and 304). Several of the national museum's painting, Buddhist art and crafts rooms are closed until January 28, 2027, so check its notice before you build a route around a specific work.

faq.q: Is Leeum free, and do I need a reservation?
faq.a: Leeum's traditional art permanent exhibition and the Gabriel Orozco Garden are free; special exhibitions are paid. Booking is optional: online tickets open 14 days ahead, up to four per person, and you can also get tickets at the desk, though the museum warns of waits on busy days. It closes on Mondays.

faq.q: Which art museums are open on Mondays in Seoul?
faq.a: MMCA Seoul opens every day except January 1, Seollal and Chuseok, and the National Museum of Korea opens on Mondays except the first Monday of March, June, September and December (December 7 in 2026). Leeum, SeMA and MMCA Deoksugung close on Mondays, though SeMA opens when a Monday is a public holiday.

faq.q: When is MMCA free?
faq.a: Paid exhibitions at MMCA Seoul and MMCA Deoksugung are free on Wednesday and Saturday evenings from 18:00 to 21:00 and on the last Wednesday of each month. Visitors under 24 or over 65 enter free at any time with ID. At Deoksugung you still pay the palace's own fee, and its gate stops admitting visitors at 20:00.

faq.q: Where can I see paintings by Chun Kyung-ja?
faq.a: At the Seoul Museum of Art's Seosomun main building near Deoksugung, which has a permanent Chun Kyung-ja collection room on the second floor. She donated 93 works to the museum in 1998, and the current centenary display shows about 30 of them. Admission is free; the building closes on Mondays.
